qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: A second, mirrored opinion clause that casts the narrator: after one clause says how someone sees another person (they see him as a hero, I think her a genius), a following clause with its own subject says how people see me or us (and she thinks me a fool, but the children saw us as giants); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', firing most with the verbs see, think and regard. Weak when the second clause casts him, her, you or them, when me is cast with no earlier opinion clause, when me is cast in the first clause and answers back, with the verbs treat, view or consider, and when an institution (the press, the company) does the seeing.
fire: My father sees my brother as a hero, and my mother sees me as a troublemaker.
They think her a genius, but she thinks me a fool.
The parents saw the teacher as a stranger, but the children saw us as giants.
He regards his sister as a saint, while she regards me as a nuisance.
Everyone in town sees him as a villain, yet his dog still sees me as a friend.
The coach thought Marco a natural, and the captain thought me a liability.
Grandma saw Lily as an angel, but Grandpa saw us as little rascals.
You think him a bore, and he probably thinks me a snob.
